sections.title: The Presumption of Purity
sections.html:
Every woman who has become pure through a proper tevila (immersion) is under a presumption of purity for her husband, and she may have union with her husband without any bedika (internal examination) and without concern that perhaps she has seen blood. On the contrary, the Sages said (Nidda 12a) that it is preferable that she not examine herself before union, so that her husband's heart not trouble him – that perhaps his wife is examining because she felt that her veset (menstrual period) had begun, and did not see blood in her bedika because she did not examine well, or because the blood dissolved and was lost, or because the bleeding has not yet begun but will begin during the union. After union too it is preferable that she not examine, because it is not fitting to raise doubts about the mitzva of ona (the marital mitzva) that they have already fulfilled, lest their hearts trouble them in the future so that they become apprehensive about fulfilling the mitzva. This is what the Sages said (Nidda 15a): "All women are under a presumption of purity for their husbands," and even "those who come back from a journey – their wives are under a presumption of purity for them." The husband should not be concerned that perhaps, while he was far from home, his wife did not attend to her purity and perhaps saw blood without being aware of it; therefore, even when she is asleep, he may come and lie beside her. But at the ona (time period) of her veset, that is, at the time when there is a reasonable concern that she will get her veset, they must refrain from union, as will be explained in the following halakhot.1

However, not close to union and unconnected with it, it is a virtue for a woman to examine herself frequently, because at times it happens that the veset arrives at an unexpected time, and through these bedikot she will know of it (Nidda 13a). In the past, when means of wiping were less available, and there were no toilet rooms in which one could relieve oneself comfortably and in privacy, only women who were meticulous about their cleanliness and purity examined themselves every time they relieved themselves. But nowadays almost all women are meticulous in this, in that they look at the panty liner, or at the toilet paper with which they wiped after relieving themselves in the toilet, and through this they know whether the veset has begun. However, a woman who is liable to see ketamim (bloodstains; singular ketem) during her days of purity, because of wounds she has, or because of an intrauterine device or hormonal pills or for other reasons, would do better not to look at the toilet paper at the beginning of wiping, so that her heart not trouble her over ketamim. For the purpose of these bedikot is to know whether an unexpected veset has arrived, and not to check whether there are ketamim.2

sections.title: The Mitzva of Separation at the Time of Concern for the Veset
sections.html:
The Sages said (Shevu'ot 18b) that there is a mitzva for the couple to refrain from union during the ona in which the woman is liable to get her veset, as it is stated (Vayikra 15:31): "Thus you shall keep apart (that is, separate) the children of Israel from their impurity, so that they not die in their impurity when they defile My Tabernacle that is in their midst." Therefore the Sages instituted that when the ona arrives in which the woman is liable to see her veset, the couple should refrain from union, lest the veset begin during the union. An ona is a day or a night (as explained below, section 4).

A few verses after the mitzva to separate Israel from their impurity, it is stated (Vayikra 16:1): "And the Lord spoke to Moshe after the death of the two sons of Aharon, when they drew near before the Lord and died," to teach us that even a great and righteous person may be punished if he is not careful to withdraw from holiness at a time when this is necessary (see Shevu'ot 18b). The intention of Aharon's sons was good – they wished to draw close to God – but they breached the boundary and died. As it is stated (Vayikra 10:1-2): "And the sons of Aharon, Nadav and Avihu, each took his fire pan, and put fire in it, and laid incense on it, and offered strange fire before the Lord, which He had not commanded them. And fire went out from before the Lord and consumed them, and they died before the Lord." Similarly, the mitzva of ona is a mitzva through which the Shekhina (Divine Presence) dwells (Sota 17a; Ramban in Iggeret Ha-kodesh). But when it is done without care to avoid the prohibition, it renders them impure and removes the Shekhina from among them. And concerning this the Torah warned: "Thus you shall keep apart (that is, separate) the children of Israel from their impurity, so that they not die in their impurity when they defile My Tabernacle that is in their midst."

A couple who sanctify themselves in the mitzva of ona, that is, who fulfill the mitzva with joy, out of faithfulness and love, and at the same time are careful to separate at the ona of the veset – will merit children who know how to restrain themselves and to add goodness and blessing. Their sons will be men of understanding, responsible and diligent, and fit to give rulings in Torah. And their daughters will be women of insight, fit to absorb the word of God and to reveal it throughout the expanses of life (based on Shevu'ot 18b).3

sections.title: The Laws of Separation
sections.html:
The mitzva of separation is to refrain from union, but hugging and kissing out of affection are permitted, because the Sages forbade only union, lest the veset begin during the union. However, a couple who are concerned that hugging might lead them to the prohibition of union, or that the husband might come to emit seed in vain, must refrain from hugging as well.4

Toward the end of the ona the woman must examine herself with an internal bedika in the vagina, to know whether the veset has begun. In a night ona she should examine herself after she gets up (the manner of the bedika is explained above 4:3). And if she did not examine herself at the end of the ona, after a fixed veset or an ona beinonit (the "average ona", explained below in section 5), they should not have union until she examines and sees that she is clean (SA YD 189:4).5

sections.title: The Duration of the Ona of Separation
sections.html:
The mitzva of separation is during the 'ona' in which it is likely that the woman will get her veset. Women who have a veset kavu'a (fixed veset), that is, whose cycle has appeared precisely three times in succession, must separate during the ona in which the veset is due to appear (as explained in section 6). And women who do not have a fixed veset must separate during the three onot in which there is a greater chance that the veset may appear (as explained in the next section).

An 'ona' is a day or a night. The day ona is from sunrise until sunset, and the night ona from sunset until sunrise. If the previous veset began by day – the separation must be in a day ona; if the previous veset began at night – the separation must be in a night ona. Even a woman who usually gets her veset at the beginning of the ona or at its end must separate throughout the entire ona, but in the ona before it or after it she need not separate. And although some hold that le-khatḥila it is good to be stringent and separate also one ona before, the halakha follows the view of the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim, that one must separate for one ona only.6

sections.title: Separation for a Veset That Is Not Fixed
sections.html:
A woman who does not have a fixed veset must separate during the three onot in which there is a greater chance that her veset will begin: a) onat ha-haflaga (the ona of the interval); b) ona beinonit (the average ona); c) onat ha-ḥodesh (the monthly ona). These three onot are calculated from the last veset, but the one before it is not taken into account (SA YD 189:1; Rema 13). At times one must also be concerned for veset ha-guf (a bodily veset), that is, distinct physical signs that appear before the veset, as explained below (section 7).

Explanation of the three onot: a) Onat ha-haflaga, that is, the interval between the last veset and the one that preceded it, because at times the veset appears in a cycle of intervals. For example, if thirty-five days passed between the last cycle and the one that preceded it, there is a chance that so it will be the next time as well. Therefore one should count thirty-five days from the previous cycle and observe the ona of separation of the haflaga. b) Ona beinonit, that is, thirty days after the previous veset, because it is common for the veset to appear in a thirty-day cycle. In the count of thirty days, the day of the previous seeing is counted as the first day, and the day on which one must separate as the thirtieth day. In practice the ona beinonit always falls after four weeks and one day. For if the previous veset was on Sunday, in the day ona, after four weeks and a day, that is, on Monday in the day ona, the time of the ona beinonit will arrive. c) Onat ha-ḥodesh, that is, on the same day and ona in the following month, because at times the veset appears according to the cycle of the moon, by which the Hebrew month is determined. For example, if in the previous month the veset appeared on the 3rd of the month, one must separate in the following month on the 3rd of the month. It should be noted that when the previous month was ḥaser (29 days), the 'onat ha-ḥodesh' and the 'ona beinonit' will fall in the same ona. When the previous month was malei (30 days), the 'onat ha-ḥodesh' will come one day after the 'ona beinonit'.

As we have learned, an ona is a day or a night; it emerges that if the previous veset began by day, as happens many times, all three onot in which one must separate fall in the day ona. If the previous veset began at night, all three onot fall in the night ona.

sections.title: Separation for a Fixed Veset
sections.html:
For a woman who has a fixed veset, the ona of separation is one ona only, in which she is due to get the next veset. A fixed veset is established by its appearance in a fixed cycle three times in succession. There are various kinds of fixity: a 'veset ha-haflaga' (interval veset) is established after there was an equal interval between the vestot three times in succession, for example after thirty-five days in the day ona; from then on they must always separate thirty-five days after the previous veset, in the day ona. A 'veset ha-ḥodesh' (monthly veset) is established after the veset appeared three times in succession on the same date of the Hebrew month and in the same ona; from then on they must separate every month on that date and in that ona. And so too anything similar: whenever the veset appeared three times in a fixed cycle, the woman has established a veset for herself, and from then on they must separate only at the ona of her fixed veset.

A woman who had a fixed veset and changed, and saw not at the time of her fixed veset, should the next time be concerned for three onot: a) for the fixed veset; b) for the onat ha-ḥodesh from the last seeing; c) for the onat ha-haflaga from the last seeing. But she is not concerned for the ona beinonit, since the law of separation at the ona beinonit exists only for a woman who has no fixed veset. And if three times in succession she sees not in accordance with her fixed pattern, her fixed veset is cancelled, and her law reverts to the law of a woman who has no fixed veset.7

At times a woman has a 'semi-fixed' veset, according to which she does not know on which day she will see, but she does know that the length of her cycle is at most twenty-nine days, or at least thirty-two days. Then she must be concerned only for the calculation of the previous haflaga, and not for the 'ona beinonit' or the 'onat ha-ḥodesh', since these onot fall on days on which she knows she will not see. A 'semi-fixed' veset is established on the basis of three consecutive cycles.8

sections.title: Veset Ha-guf
sections.html:
A woman who felt, shortly before the appearance of her cycle, a special physical sensation, such as pains in the abdomen, the back or the head, or a sensation of particular heaviness in one of her limbs, must be concerned for a veset ha-guf (bodily veset). That is, it is possible that these sensations are the distinct signs that the veset is about to arrive; then, in the following month, when she feels this, she should separate until the end of that ona. In addition, since she has not yet established the 'veset ha-guf', she must also be concerned for the three onot explained in section 5 (SA YD 189:19, 26). If she felt the special physical sensation again and her veset did not arrive, she need no longer be concerned for it.

If during three consecutive vestot the veset began after she felt that same sensation, she has established a veset ha-guf, and she need no longer be concerned for the other onot for which she was concerned in the past (Knesset Yeḥezkel 36; Darkhei Tahara 7:72-74). If, after she established the veset ha-guf, she felt her special sensation and the cycle did not arrive in the ona in which it was due to begin, in the following month she must separate both at the ona of the 'veset ha-guf' and at the onat ha-ḥodesh and the haflaga from the previous veset. And if three consecutive times pass in which she feels her special sensation and the veset does not arrive at its ona, her veset ha-guf is uprooted (SA 189:19-26).

There are women whose veset ha-guf heralds that the cycle will begin not in the current ona but in the one after it; then they must separate in the ona in which the veset is due to appear. At times the veset ha-guf heralds that the cycle will appear in another two or three days; then, if the ona of its appearance is distinct – a day ona or a night ona – one must separate in that ona only. And if the ona of its appearance is not distinct, but rather it will be in one of two onot, one must separate in both onot in which it may appear. But if the veset ha-guf does not point to one of two onot in which it will appear, but rather there is a chance that it will appear in one of three onot, this is not a veset ha-guf, and one need not be concerned for it.

The appearance of ketamim a few hours before the beginning of the veset can also be considered a veset ha-guf. That is, even though the ketamim themselves do not render impure, because they were on a colored garment and the like (above 2:7-9), since they contain a sign that the veset is about to arrive in that ona, when they appear again in the following month the couple must separate until the end of that ona. Usually these ketamim appear together with certain sensations, and then they are considered a veset ha-guf only when they appear with those same sensations. These sensations need not be defined; the main thing is that the woman knows that the ketem in combination with these sensations is a sign that the veset is about to appear.9

sections.title: Some Laws of Vestot
sections.html:
The veset usually lasts several days, whether in a flow or in spurts that stop and resume; however, the ona of the veset is determined according to the time at which the veset begins (SA YD 184:6; Rema 189:13).

Vestot are established by blood that came out with sensation in the manner of a veset, and not by ketamim, even if they render impure (Ra'avad; SA 190:54).10

A woman who was negligent in keeping the calculation of her ona of separation, and does not know when she must separate – whether she had a fixed veset or did not have a fixed veset – is permitted on all days. Because the obligation of separation at the ona close to the veset is from the words of the Sages, and in a doubt concerning the words of the Sages the halakha is to be lenient (Ḥavot Da'at 184:4; Minḥat Pitim; see Ḥatam Sofer YD 166). However, so that such a mishap not occur, every woman must keep an exact record of the time at which she gets her veset each month, and, if it appeared with special sensations, note those as well, so that she will know when she must separate, and also be able to know whether she has a fixed veset.

sections.title: One Who Sets Out on a Journey
sections.html:
It is a mitzva for a man who must travel away from home for several days to "visit" his wife, that is, to be with her, on the night before his journey. For the mitzva of ona requires fulfilling union at the fixed times, and in addition at a time when the desire of one of the spouses intensifies. By the nature of the world, before the husband is about to travel away from home their desire intensifies, and therefore they are obligated to have union on the night before his journey, so that they part with love and joy. And so is the law when the wife must travel away from home for several days.

The Sages said that by virtue of union on the night before the journey, they will merit to keep faith with one another and will not sin during their separation in thought or in deed of betrayal, as it is stated (Iyov 5:24): "And you shall know that your tent is at peace, and you shall visit your habitation and shall not sin." Since this mitzva is great and important, the Sages said that it is a mitzva to have union even if the night before the husband's departure falls in the ona in which they must separate. For as long as she has not actually felt that the veset has begun, by Torah law they are permitted, and it was the Sages who established that it is a mitzva to separate at the ona of the veset; and since the obligation to have union before the journey is from the Torah, it overrides the mitzva of separation at the ona of the veset, which is from the words of the Sages.

However, some of the Rishonim were stringent and ruled that if the night before the journey falls in the ona of separation, union is forbidden, and the mitzva is rather to increase in words of affection and love (Rabbeinu Tam and the Rosh). But according to most poskim, even if the night before the journey falls in the ona of separation, they should have union. However, when possible, it is better to set the time of departure not in the ona of separation (Maharshal, Torat Ha-shelamim). When the journey is short, so that he will manage to return before the time of their mitzva of ona according to their regular practice arrives, they should part with a hug and a kiss and not with union.

This mitzva is unique to one who sets out on a journey, for it involves both a great obligation of the mitzva of ona and also shalom bayit (marital harmony) and protection from stumbling; but at other times when it is a mitzva to have union, even on the night of tevila, union in the ona of separation is not to be permitted.11

sections.title: Pregnant and Nursing Women – Mesulakot Damim
sections.html:
A woman who has become pregnant, as long as she has not verified this by a reliable test, must during the first three months separate at the onot of her veset like all women. But if she knows with certainty, on the basis of a pregnancy test, that she is pregnant, she is considered 'mesuleket damim' (one whose blood has ceased), and she need no longer separate at the ona of her veset. And although at times she still sees blood and becomes impure from it, this is not according to the cycle of the veset but due to bleeding that sometimes occurs at the beginning of pregnancy.12

Likewise, a nursing woman is considered 'mesuleket damim' as long as she nurses even once a day, provided that she has not yet seen her first veset and twenty-four months have not passed since the birth. But if she stopped nursing completely, or saw a veset, or twenty-four months have passed even though she is still nursing, she is not considered 'mesuleket damim', and she reverts to her previous laws. That is, if before the beginning of the pregnancy she had a fixed veset on the 3rd of the month, she should separate on the 3rd of the following month according to the law of her fixed veset. Likewise, if she had a 'veset ha-guf', when she again feels the sensation of her veset she should separate until the end of the ona, as she was accustomed. Likewise, if she was accustomed to see a fixed veset of intervals, after she sees once again she should return to observing her fixed interval veset. And if three times she did not see at the ona of her fixed veset, she is no longer concerned for it. And if she did not have a fixed veset, after she sees once she should be concerned for the three onot, in the manner of a woman who has no fixed veset.13

sections.title: The Law of a Woman Who Takes Hormonal Pills
sections.html:
A woman who takes hormonal pills that postpone the appearance of the veset, as long as she is taking the pills and according to the medical assessment she is not supposed to get a period, need not be concerned for the onot of separation, whether these are onot of separation due to a fixed veset or due to a veset that is not fixed.

After she stops taking the pills, she should separate at the ona in which she is due to get the veset. And since there are different pills, and their effect on women differs, each woman must check how long after she stops taking these pills she begins to see blood, and until she knows this, she should separate starting 48 hours after taking the last pill. Afterwards, if three times she finds that she begins to see blood after a longer time, for example three days from taking the last pill, she should establish a veset accordingly, and be concerned for the ona in which she is liable to get her period. And if she is in doubt, she should be stringent also for one ona earlier.14

sections.title: An Older Woman
sections.html:
A woman who has reached menopause, at which the veset stops appearing, and ninety days have passed without her seeing a veset, is no longer subject to the law of separation at the ona of her veset. Because even if she sees a veset, since it is no longer regular, there is no time at which it is likely that she will see the next veset. However, when she sees blood she becomes impure like all women, but she will not need to calculate from that seeing onot in which they must separate.

If, after she stopped seeing for ninety days, she again saw three vestot in a fixed cycle, she has established a fixed veset (SA YD 189:30-31). And if the veset again appeared according to the previous fixed pattern she had, even once – for example, she was accustomed to see on every 3rd of the month and again saw on the 3rd of the month – immediately after one time she must again be concerned for her fixed pattern according to the law of a fixed veset. For it has become clear that that ninety-day stop was not the stop that heralded the final cessation of the cycle of the veset.

If, after she stopped seeing for ninety days, she again saw three vestot, each month or at most every two months, without a fixed cycle, from the appearance of the third cycle she should begin to be concerned for her seeings according to the law of a veset that is not fixed.15
